title: Starting at a New School as a Teacher
author: Deb
summary: Deb draws on thirty years of teaching experience across five schools to map the emotional and practical landscape of starting at a new school as a teacher — a transition that receives far less attention than any other career transition in education. She describes the first-day experience: simultaneously navigating unfamiliar systems, building student relationships from scratch, managing staffroom politics, and negotiating the gap between who you were in your previous school and who you are as an unknown new arrival. The article covers both practical and emotional dimensions: neutrality as a default in unfamiliar terrain, the priority of student relationships over adult ones, and the particular vulnerability of being experienced but unknown. Deb argues that the emotional labour of school transitions is systematically underestimated by both the receiving institution and the teacher themselves. The piece offers concrete advice while validating how genuinely difficult the process is regardless of experience level.
points: Starting at a new school as an experienced teacher activates a particular professional anxiety: you know what you're doing, but you have to prove it all over again.
Neutrality is often the safest default position in the staffroom during the early weeks — until you fully understand the cultural and political terrain.
The priority is always the students: building rapport with the people you are there to teach is more important than navigating adult relationships and staffroom dynamics.
The emotional labour of school transitions is systematically underestimated — both by institutions welcoming new staff and by experienced teachers who believe they should be past it.
Being experienced but unknown is its own kind of professional vulnerability: you carry expertise no one has yet learned to trust, and patience is the only path through it.
quotes: By the time I finally got the code, the bell had rung, my worksheets were unprinted, and I had to improvise and use the school textbooks instead, and scrap the project I had planned to start on with my first class.

If I had had information on behaviour policy, safeguarding procedure, photocopier procedure, IT logins and my timetable earlier, I would have felt a lot more confident before I got into the classroom.
There were always procedures I was told about that weren’t in the handbook, including some systems that seemed complex, but other staff members assured me that I would get the hang of them quickly.
When I started teaching schools didn’t have websites, but now they do, so I think it would be really important for any new teacher to look at a school’s website before they have their first day.
Sometimes at the end of a lesson I would feel exhausted but there was nowhere and no time allowed for recovery when my next class had already arrived and were waiting to come into my classroom.
I taught them maths, and some learners had already decided that it really wasn’t for them.Some of the students in the class had built up a reputation of testing new teachers to the limit.
In my first week and sometimes for my first month in a new school, I was spending time learning their names, their personalities, their needs, and the dynamics of each of my classes.
